rows.reference: Qur'an 5:32 (Sūrat al-Māʾida), read with 5:33
rows.original: مَن قَتَلَ نَفْسًا بِغَيْرِ نَفْسٍ أَوْ فَسَادٍ فِي الْأَرْضِ فَكَأَنَّمَا قَتَلَ النَّاسَ جَمِيعًا
rows.translation: Pickthall (1930), recalled from memory, not checked against the page
rows.says: God decreed for the Children of Israel that whoever kills a human being, except in return for a life or for spreading corruption in the land, is as if he had killed all humankind, and whoever saves one life is as if he had saved all humankind. Verse 5:33 then sets the penalties for those who wage war on God and His Messenger and spread corruption.
rows.bearing: K1 and K0: Explicit wider rule (rule 7). 'A soul' (nafs) means any human being, so it reaches everyone K1 protects, whatever their faith, sex or status. Its two exceptions are retaliation for a life (qiṣāṣ) and 'corruption in the land', which 5:33 places among penalties; both are context (a) under rule 5, and nothing in the verse lets a private person act on them. Caveats: the verse is framed as a decree to the Children of Israel (commentators such as Ibn Kathīr are reported to apply it to all; not checked), and the reach of 'corruption in the land' is debated. A reading that let private persons kill for 'corruption' would raise rule 6; no counted text doing so was met.

rows.reference: Qur'an 6:151 (Sūrat al-Anʿām)
rows.original: وَلَا تَقْتُلُوا أَوْلَادَكُم مِّنْ إِمْلَاقٍ ... وَلَا تَقْتُلُوا النَّفْسَ الَّتِي حَرَّمَ اللَّهُ إِلَّا بِالْحَقِّ
rows.translation: Pickthall (1930), recalled from memory
rows.says: Among the things God has forbidden: do not kill your children because of poverty, for God provides for you and for them; and do not kill the soul that God has made sacred, except by right.
rows.bearing: K1: Explicit (rule 7) for children, including newborns (rule 9), and for 'the soul God has made sacred'. The exception 'by right' (bi-l-ḥaqq) is spelled out in the Sunnah (Bukhārī 6878, below) as penalties a court imposes, besides war: context (a) and (b), rule 5. Scope question: which souls God 'made sacred'. Ibn Kathīr on this verse is reported to include the believer and the covenanted non-Muslim, citing Bukhārī 3166 (not checked); classical law gave no such protection to enemy non-Muslims without a covenant, which belongs to war, context (b). K0: Explicit for killing children from fear of want (a motive of gain).

rows.reference: Qur'an 17:31 (Sūrat al-Isrāʾ)
rows.original: وَلَا تَقْتُلُوا أَوْلَادَكُمْ خَشْيَةَ إِمْلَاقٍ ... إِنَّ قَتْلَهُمْ كَانَ خِطْئًا كَبِيرًا
rows.translation: Pickthall (1930), recalled from memory
rows.says: Do not kill your children for fear of poverty; God provides for them and for you. Killing them is a great sin.
rows.bearing: K1: Explicit for children from birth (rule 9). It is addressed to parents acting on their own authority, so it reaches the household. K0: Explicit (killing to avoid the cost of a child).

rows.reference: Qur'an 17:33 (Sūrat al-Isrāʾ)
rows.original: وَلَا تَقْتُلُوا النَّفْسَ الَّتِي حَرَّمَ اللَّهُ إِلَّا بِالْحَقِّ ۗ وَمَن قُتِلَ مَظْلُومًا فَقَدْ جَعَلْنَا لِوَلِيِّهِ سُلْطَانًا فَلَا يُسْرِف فِّي الْقَتْلِ
rows.translation: Pickthall (1930), recalled from memory
rows.says: Do not kill the soul that God has made sacred, except by right. If someone is killed wrongfully, God has given his heir authority, but the heir must not go beyond the limit in killing.
rows.bearing: K1: Explicit, as 6:151 (rule 7). K0: Clear teaching against excess in revenge; commentators are reported to read 'no excess' as killing only the killer, not others or more than one (not checked). The heir's 'authority' is the right to retaliation (qiṣāṣ). Classical law is reported to require the ruler's authority to carry it out (al-Qurṭubī on 2:178 reports agreement on this; al-Qurṭubī is not on the corpus list; not checked), which makes it context (a) under rule 5. If counted texts are found that let an heir kill on his own authority without any court, the point becomes Unclear (rules 5 and 6).

rows.reference: Qur'an 25:68 to 70 (Sūrat al-Furqān)
rows.original: وَلَا يَقْتُلُونَ النَّفْسَ الَّتِي حَرَّمَ اللَّهُ إِلَّا بِالْحَقِّ
rows.translation: Pickthall (1930), recalled from memory
rows.says: The true servants of the Merciful do not call on another god, do not kill the soul God has made sacred except by right, and do not commit adultery. Whoever does these things meets a doubled penalty, unless he repents, believes and does good.
rows.bearing: K1 and K0: Explicit restatement of 6:151 and 17:33 (rule 7), with the same 'by right' exception (rule 5). The promise of forgiveness to the repentant (25:70) concerns God's judgement, not permission.

rows.reference: Qur'an 81:8 to 9 (Sūrat al-Takwīr); 16:58 to 59 (Sūrat al-Naḥl); 6:140 (Sūrat al-Anʿām)
rows.original: وَإِذَا الْمَوْءُودَةُ سُئِلَتْ ۝ بِأَيِّ ذَنبٍ قُتِلَتْ
rows.translation: Pickthall (1930), recalled from memory
rows.says: At the Judgement the girl who was buried alive will be asked for what sin she was killed (81:8 to 9). Those whose faces darken at news of a daughter, and who wonder whether to keep her in shame or bury her in the dust, judge evilly (16:58 to 59). Those who kill their children foolishly, without knowledge, are lost (6:140).
rows.bearing: K1: Explicit (6:140) and Clear teaching (81:8 to 9; 16:58 to 59) that killing newborn and infant children, girls above all, is a grave wrong (rule 9). The wrongdoers are parents acting on their own authority, so it reaches the household. K0: the motive in 16:58 to 59 is shame, close to the anger and hatred K0 names.

rows.original: وَلَا يَقْتُلْنَ أَوْلَادَهُنَّ
rows.translation: Pickthall (1930), recalled from memory
rows.says: The pledge the Prophet took from believing women included that they would not kill their children.
rows.bearing: K1: Explicit for children (rule 9); binds mothers, so reaches the household.

rows.reference: Qur'an 4:92 to 93 (Sūrat al-Nisāʾ)
rows.original: وَمَا كَانَ لِمُؤْمِنٍ أَن يَقْتُلَ مُؤْمِنًا إِلَّا خَطَأً ... وَمَن يَقْتُلْ مُؤْمِنًا مُّتَعَمِّدًا فَجَزَاؤُهُ جَهَنَّمُ
rows.translation: Pickthall (1930), recalled from memory
rows.says: A believer may never kill a believer, except by mistake. Accidental killing requires compensation to the family and freeing a believing slave (or two months' fasting), including where the victim's people have a treaty with the Muslims. Whoever kills a believer deliberately, his reward is Hell, with God's anger and curse.
rows.bearing: K1 and K0: Explicit, but owed to believers only, so taught in part (rule 7). Most of 4:92 concerns accidental killing, context (f); its treaty clause shows compensation reaching treaty peoples for accidental killing. The threat for deliberate killing (4:93) is among the strongest in the Qur'an.
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: no search could be run (shared search limit used up); from memory. 4:92 was also left unverified in the households annex (IS-5). To check at quran.com/4/92-93.

rows.reference: Qur'an 4:29 to 30 (Sūrat al-Nisāʾ)
rows.original: وَلَا تَقْتُلُوا أَنفُسَكُمْ ... وَمَن يَفْعَلْ ذَٰلِكَ عُدْوَانًا وَظُلْمًا فَسَوْفَ نُصْلِيهِ نَارًا
rows.translation: Pickthall (1930) 'kill not one another'; Sahih International 'do not kill yourselves (or one another)'; both recalled from memory
rows.says: Do not consume one another's wealth unjustly, only by trade with mutual consent, and do not kill one another (or: yourselves). Whoever does so in aggression and injustice will be cast into the Fire.
rows.bearing: K1: Explicit if read as 'one another', and addressed to believers (taught in part, rule 7). The word anfusakum can also mean 'yourselves', which commentators read as forbidding suicide: context (d). Translation changes the meaning here. K0: Clear teaching, since the verse joins the ban to taking wealth unjustly and names aggression and injustice as the wrong motive.

rows.reference: Qur'an 5:27 to 31 (Sūrat al-Māʾida), the two sons of Adam
rows.original: لَئِن بَسَطتَ إِلَيَّ يَدَكَ لِتَقْتُلَنِي مَا أَنَا بِبَاسِطٍ يَدِيَ إِلَيْكَ لِأَقْتُلَكَ
rows.translation: Pickthall (1930), recalled from memory
rows.says: God accepted one son's offering and not the other's, and the rejected son threatened to kill his brother. The brother replied that even if he raised his hand to kill him, he would not raise his own to kill in return, for he feared God. The killer's soul made the murder seem easy; he killed his brother and became one of the losers, full of regret. Verse 32 begins 'For that cause'.
rows.bearing: K0: Clear teaching that killing from envy and anger is a grave wrong (rule 7). K1: Clear teaching (an innocent victim; the story is the stated ground of 5:32). The brother's refusal to defend himself asks more than K1, which permits but does not require defence; it does not contradict K1.

rows.reference: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 6878 (Book of Blood Money, Kitāb al-Diyāt); Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 1676 (Kitāb al-Qasāma); Forty Hadith of an-Nawawī no. 14 (ʿAbd al-Bāqī numbering as on Sunnah.com; older English numbering not recorded)
rows.original: لَا يَحِلُّ دَمُ امْرِئٍ مُسْلِمٍ ... إِلَّا بِإِحْدَى ثَلَاثٍ: النَّفْسُ بِالنَّفْسِ، وَالثَّيِّبُ الزَّانِي، وَالْمَارِقُ مِنَ الدِّينِ التَّارِكُ لِلْجَمَاعَةِ
rows.translation: M. Muhsin Khan (Sunnah.com), recalled from memory
rows.says: The blood of a Muslim who bears witness to God and His Messenger may not be shed except in three cases: a life for a life, a married person who commits adultery, and one who leaves the religion and abandons the community.
rows.bearing: K1: Explicit for Muslims only, so taught in part (rule 7). It spells out the Qur'an's 'by right' narrowly, and all three cases are penalties that classical law gives to a court and ruler: context (a), rule 5. Ibn Rajab (Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm wa-l-Ḥikam, on no. 14) and al-Nawawī are reported to discuss these cases and who carries them out (not checked).

rows.reference: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 3166 (Book of Jizya, Book 58, hadith 8); parallel 6914
rows.original: مَنْ قَتَلَ مُعَاهَدًا لَمْ يَرِحْ رَائِحَةَ الْجَنَّةِ
rows.translation: M. Muhsin Khan (Sunnah.com)
rows.says: Whoever kills a person who has a treaty or covenant with the Muslims (muʿāhad, a protected non-Muslim) will not smell the fragrance of Paradise, though it can be smelt from forty years' distance.
rows.bearing: K1: Explicit for non-Muslims under covenant (rule 7). With the rows on believers it extends protection across faiths, but not to non-Muslims with no covenant, so on its own it is taught in part.

rows.reference: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 2766 (Book of Wills); Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 89 (Book of Faith)
rows.original: اجْتَنِبُوا السَّبْعَ الْمُوبِقَاتِ ... وَقَتْلُ النَّفْسِ الَّتِي حَرَّمَ اللَّهُ إِلَّا بِالْحَقِّ
rows.translation: M. Muhsin Khan (Sunnah.com), recalled from memory
rows.says: Avoid the seven destroying sins, among them killing the soul God has made sacred, except by right.
rows.bearing: K1 and K0: Explicit; repeats the Qur'anic wording and its exception (rules 5 and 7). Adds weight, not scope.

rows.reference: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 6862 and 6864 (Book of Blood Money); 6864 = Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 1678
rows.original: لَنْ يَزَالَ الْمُؤْمِنُ فِي فُسْحَةٍ مِنْ دِينِهِ مَا لَمْ يُصِبْ دَمًا حَرَامًا؛ أَوَّلُ مَا يُقْضَى بَيْنَ النَّاسِ فِي الدِّمَاءِ
rows.translation: M. Muhsin Khan (Sunnah.com), recalled from memory
rows.says: A believer keeps the room his religion gives him until he sheds blood that is forbidden (6862). The first cases judged between people on the Day of Resurrection are cases of blood (6864).
rows.bearing: K1: Explicit (6862) and Clear teaching (6864, 'between people', with no limit of faith) that unlawful killing is among the gravest wrongs (rule 7). Adds weight; the scope still depends on what blood is 'forbidden'.

rows.reference: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 4477 (Book of Tafsir, on 2:22); Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 86 (Book of Faith); parallels elsewhere in Bukhārī (numbers not confirmed)
rows.original: أَنْ تَقْتُلَ وَلَدَكَ تَخَافُ أَنْ يَطْعَمَ مَعَكَ
rows.translation: M. Muhsin Khan (Sunnah.com), recalled from memory

rows.reference: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 5975 (Book of Good Manners); parallel 2408
rows.original: إِنَّ اللَّهَ حَرَّمَ عَلَيْكُمْ عُقُوقَ الأُمَّهَاتِ، وَوَأْدَ الْبَنَاتِ
rows.translation: M. Muhsin Khan (Sunnah.com), recalled from memory
rows.says: God has forbidden you to be undutiful to mothers and to bury daughters alive, among other things.
rows.bearing: K1: Explicit for newborn girls (rule 9), binding parents.

rows.tier: 2 (Sunni) for the hadith; 1 (all branches) for Qur'an 24:6 to 9
rows.branch: Sunni for the hadith; all branches for the verses
rows.reference: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 1498a and 1498b (Book of Liʿān); Qur'an 24:6 to 9 (Sūrat al-Nūr); Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 5259 (Book of Divorce) and 4745 (Tafsir of Sūrat al-Nūr), the case of ʿUwaymir al-ʿAjlānī
rows.original: لَوْ وَجَدْتُ مَعَ أَهْلِي رَجُلًا لَمْ أَمَسَّهُ حَتَّى آتِيَ بِأَرْبَعَةِ شُهَدَاءَ؟ قَالَ: نَعَمْ؛ أَيَقْتُلُهُ فَتَقْتُلُونَهُ
rows.translation: A. H. Siddiqui (Muslim) and M. Muhsin Khan (Bukhārī), on Sunnah.com; Pickthall for the verses; all recalled from memory
rows.says: Saʿd ibn ʿUbāda asked whether, if he found a man with his wife, he must not touch him until he brought four witnesses; the Prophet said yes (1498a; 1498b: 'give him respite'). ʿUwaymir asked what a man should do who finds another man with his wife: 'should he kill him, and then you kill him?' The answer was the procedure of mutual oaths (liʿān, 24:6 to 9), which ends in separation, not killing.
rows.bearing: K1: Explicit (1498a) and Clear teaching (24:6 to 9 with Bukhārī 5259) that a husband may not kill his wife or her lover on his own authority (rule 7); the question in 5259 assumes such a killing would bring retaliation, and the Prophet does not correct it. Reaches the household (husbands). K0: Clear teaching against killing from jealous anger. See the next row for the other side.
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: no search could be run (shared search limit used up); from memory. To check at sunnah.com/muslim:1498a, sunnah.com/bukhari:5259 and quran.com/24/6-9.

rows.reference: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 1498c; Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 6846 (with its chapter heading)
rows.original: أَتَعْجَبُونَ مِنْ غَيْرَةِ سَعْدٍ؟ وَاللَّهِ لَأَنَا أَغْيَرُ مِنْهُ، وَاللَّهُ أَغْيَرُ مِنِّي
rows.translation: A. H. Siddiqui and M. Muhsin Khan (Sunnah.com), recalled from memory
rows.says: Saʿd said he would strike such a man with the sword before fetching witnesses. The Prophet said: listen to what your leader says; he is jealous, I am more jealous than he, and God is more jealous than I. Bukhārī places a version under a heading about a man who finds another with his wife and kills him, without stating a ruling.
rows.bearing: Praises protective jealousy (ghayra) but does not say the killing would be right, so under rule 4 it does not decide. Al-Nawawī and Ibn Ḥajar are reported to read it as praise of jealousy with the ruling of 1498a standing, and most classical jurists as holding a husband who kills without proof liable to retaliation (not checked). A limit to record, not a contradiction.
rows.verification: UNVERIFIED: no search could be run (shared search limit used up); from memory. To check at sunnah.com/muslim:1498c and sunnah.com/bukhari:6846.

rows.reference: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 1218a (Book of Pilgrimage; Jābir's account of the Farewell Sermon)
rows.original: إِنَّ دِمَاءَكُمْ وَأَمْوَالَكُمْ حَرَامٌ عَلَيْكُمْ ... وَدِمَاءُ الْجَاهِلِيَّةِ مَوْضُوعَةٌ
rows.translation: A. H. Siddiqui (Sunnah.com), recalled from memory
rows.says: Your blood and your property are sacred to one another, as this day is sacred. The blood claims of the age before Islam are cancelled, and the first the Prophet cancels is a claim of his own family (the blood of Ibn Rabīʿa ibn al-Ḥārith).
rows.bearing: K0: Clear teaching against blood feud: old claims to revenge are cancelled, starting with the Prophet's own kin (rule 7). K1: Explicit, but addressed to the Muslim gathering, so taught in part.

rows.tier: 2 (Shia; highly revered, not treated as authoritative by most Sunni scholars)
rows.reference: Nahj al-Balāgha, Letter 53 (ʿAlī to Mālik al-Ashtar on appointing him governor of Egypt)
rows.original: إِيَّاكَ وَالدِّمَاءَ وَسَفْكَهَا بِغَيْرِ حِلِّهَا؛ فَإِنَّهُمْ صِنْفَانِ: إِمَّا أَخٌ لَكَ فِي الدِّينِ، وَإِمَّا نَظِيرٌ لَكَ فِي الْخَلْقِ
rows.translation: Translation on al-islam.org, recalled from memory
rows.says: Beware of shedding blood without right: nothing brings punishment and the loss of blessing sooner, and God will begin His judgement between His servants on the Day of Resurrection with the blood they shed. Earlier in the letter: the people are of two kinds, your brother in religion or your equal in creation, so show mercy to all.
rows.bearing: K1: Explicit, and its 'two kinds' clause gives universal scope (rule 7). It is addressed to a governor, so it binds those who hold power. It agrees with Qur'an 5:32, so it can speak for Shia Islam under the branch rule, filling the gap left by the Sunni-only hadith rows.

rows.reference: Qur'an 4:94 (Sūrat al-Nisāʾ); Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 4269 (Book of Military Expeditions); Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 96 (Book of Faith), Usāma ibn Zayd
rows.original: وَلَا تَقُولُوا لِمَنْ أَلْقَىٰ إِلَيْكُمُ السَّلَامَ لَسْتَ مُؤْمِنًا تَبْتَغُونَ عَرَضَ الْحَيَاةِ الدُّنْيَا؛ أَفَلَا شَقَقْتَ عَنْ قَلْبِهِ
rows.translation: Pickthall (verse); Muhsin Khan and Siddiqui (hadith); recalled from memory
rows.says: When you go out in God's cause, make sure; do not say to one who offers you peace 'you are not a believer', seeking the goods of this life (4:94). Usāma ibn Zayd killed a man in battle after the man said there is no god but God; the Prophet rebuked him again and again: 'Did you cut open his heart?'
rows.bearing: K3: Explicit that a person who offers peace or submission must not be killed (war context, rule 5). K0: Clear teaching against killing for plunder. Does not decide K1 (war).

support.reconciliation:
How Islam reconciles its texts on killing, with each authority's standing.

1. The general rule. The Qur'an (Tier 1, all branches) forbids killing in general terms: any soul (5:32), 'the soul God has made sacred, except by right' (6:151, 17:33, 25:68), and one's children (6:151, 17:31, 60:12, 81:8 to 9). The Sunnah (counted for Sunni Islam) defines 'by right' narrowly. A Muslim's blood may be shed only for a life taken, adultery by a married person, or leaving the faith and the community (Bukhārī 6878 = Muslim 1676 = Forty no. 14). Classical law gives all three to a court and ruler. Al-Qurṭubī, a classical commentator not on the corpus list, is reported to record agreement that only those in authority carry out retaliation (not checked). Ibn Rajab's commentary on Forty no. 14 (a listed reconciling authority) is reported to discuss these limits (not checked). So the main exceptions fall under context (a). Self-defence is allowed against one who attacks you (Muslim 140), and classical jurists are reported to require the least force needed (al-Nawawī, listed; not checked).

2. Who is protected. The Qur'an speaks of 'a soul'. Bukhārī 3166 (verified) brings covenanted non-Muslims explicitly inside the ban. Ibn Kathīr (listed) is reported to read 6:151 that way (not checked). Qur'an 5:8 and 60:8 (verified) forbid injustice to hated and non-hostile non-Muslims. Equal liability in court is not given: Bukhārī 6915 (verified) bars retaliation against a Muslim for killing a non-Muslim in the majority view, with the Hanafi school dissenting (secondary sources only). In the same way, 2:178 is read as no retaliation on a free person for a slave, and Tirmidhī 1400 (grade to confirm) bars retaliation against a father for his child. Under rule 2 these are graded protection, not permission: the act stays forbidden and is punished by compensation and discretionary penalties. Non-Muslims with no covenant from enemy lands were unprotected in classical law, which the tradition places under the law of war, context (b).

3. Households. Husbands may not kill a wife or her lover on their own authority. Muslim 1498a requires four witnesses, and the oath procedure of Qur'an 24:6 to 9 replaces killing (Bukhārī 5259). The Prophet's praise of Saʿd's jealousy (Muslim 1498c; Bukhārī 6846) is reported to be read by al-Nawawī and Ibn Ḥajar (both listed) as praise of jealousy, not permission to kill (not checked). Parents are forbidden to kill children in many verses and hadith. Masters: Samura's hadith (Abū Dāwūd 4515; Tirmidhī 1414) would forbid killing one's slave, but its grading is disputed.

4. Unresolved hard text. Abū Dāwūd 4361 (Sunni; reported as graded ṣaḥīḥ by al-Albānī) has the Prophet declaring 'not to be avenged' a master's private killing of his slave woman for insulting the Prophet. Classical jurists are reported to have used it to treat such a person's blood as forfeit. Most are reported to hold that the penalty belongs to the ruler, so a private killer may receive a discretionary punishment for acting without authority but not retaliation. Ibn Taymiyya's al-Ṣārim al-Maslūl is outside the corpus list, and none of this was checked. No reconciliation by a listed authority was verified. Shia material on the same question (al-Kāfī) was not checked.

5. War. Qur'an 2:190 forbids transgression, and Bukhārī 3015, Muslim 1731 and Abū Dāwūd 2669 forbid killing women, children and hired workers. Bukhārī 3012 (night raids) is reported to be read as unintended harm. Qur'an 47:4 (verified) frees or ransoms captives, though classical law also let a ruler execute some captives, and the Qurayẓa judgement (Bukhārī 3043) executed surrendered fighters for breach of treaty. Shia sources (Nahj al-Balāgha Letter 14; al-Kāfī, Kitāb al-Jihād) give parallel limits. Standing: the Qur'an binds all branches. Bukhārī and Muslim bind Sunni Islam. Abū Dāwūd and al-Tirmidhī bind Sunni Islam only where graded sound or good. Nahj al-Balāgha and al-Kāfī speak for Shia Islam. The commentators are for reconciliation only.

K1.label: Provisionally Taught (all branches, through Tier 1), pending verification; on verified texts alone, only Taught in part (Sunni); at risk of Contradicted in one branch (Sunni) or Unclear
K1.reason: If the Tier 1 rows verify, Qur'an 5:32 is an Explicit universal ban ('a soul') whose exceptions are context (a) (rules 5 and 7). 6:151, 17:31, 17:33, 25:68, 60:12 and 81:8 to 9 cover children from birth (rule 9) and bind parents, and Muslim 1498a with 24:6 to 9 binds husbands. Bukhārī 3166 (verified) covers covenanted non-Muslims, and Nahj al-Balāgha Letter 53 gives the Shia branch its own universal text. The unequal penalties (Bukhārī 6915, verified; 2:178; Tirmidhī 1400) are graded protection, not contradiction (rule 2). Rule 1 bars unverified texts from deciding, and only Bukhārī 3166 among the counted texts on killing is verified, so on present evidence the result is only Taught in part (Sunni). The main threat is Abū Dāwūd 4361: a master's private killing of a slave woman who insulted the Prophet, declared not to be avenged. If its ṣaḥīḥ grade and content are confirmed, rule 3 gives Contradicted in one branch (Sunni). If the tradition treats the Prophet's declaration as a judicial ruling, rules 5 and 6 give Unclear. If al-Kāfī is found to allow the hearer of such an insult to kill, the result could become Contradicted (rule 2). The heir's role in retaliation (17:33) and private killing of apostates are further hard cases for rule 5.

K0.label: Provisionally Taught (all branches, through Tier 1), pending verification; same risk from Abū Dāwūd 4361
K0.reason: Pending verification, the Qur'an teaches K0 Explicitly or by Clear teaching. The general bans apply (5:32, 6:151, 17:33, 25:68). Killing children for fear of cost is named (6:151, 17:31; Bukhārī 4477). Killing out of envy is condemned (5:27 to 31). The ban is joined to aggression and taking wealth unjustly (4:29 to 30), and to killing for plunder (4:94). Excess in revenge is forbidden (17:33). The Farewell Sermon (Muslim 1218a, this passage unverified) cancels blood feud. Retaliation (qiṣāṣ) is revenge through a court, so it is context (a), not private revenge (rule 5). Only Implied or Tier 2 verified texts bear on K0 at present, so nothing decides it yet (rule 1). Abū Dāwūd 4361 would contradict K0 for Sunni Islam only if killing to punish an insult counts as anger or revenge. That reading is plausible but disputed, which suggests Unclear (rule 6) if the text is confirmed.

K3.label: Provisionally Taught in part: Explicit for women, children and those who offer peace (Sunni and Shia texts); contested for surrendered fighters and captives
K3.reason: Pending verification, Bukhārī 3015, Muslim 1731a and Abū Dāwūd 2669 (Sunni) and Nahj al-Balāgha Letter 14 (Shia) forbid killing women, children, hired workers, those who flee and the wounded. Qur'an 4:94 with Bukhārī 4269 and Muslim 96 forbids killing one who offers peace. Qur'an 2:190 forbids transgression, 9:6 protects those who ask for safety, and 47:4 (verified) frees or ransoms captives. The old are covered only in al-Kāfī (unconfirmed) and in hadith reported to be weak (Abū Dāwūd 2614) or outside the corpus (the Muwaṭṭaʾ). Against K3, the Qurayẓa judgement (Bukhārī 3043; Muslim 1768) executed men who had surrendered, and classical law let rulers execute some captives. Bukhārī 3012 concerns unintended harm in night raids. K3 is a record wording, so no floor depends on it.

rows.reference: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 6922 (Book of Dealing with Apostates; chapter on asking apostates to repent)
rows.original: مَنْ بَدَّلَ دِينَهُ فَاقْتُلُوهُ
rows.translation: M. Muhsin Khan, on Sunnah.com
rows.says: ʿAlī, then caliph, burned some people. Ibn ʿAbbās says he would not have burned them, because punishing with fire is forbidden, but would have killed them, because the Prophet said: whoever changes his religion, kill him.
rows.bearing: This is a death penalty for leaving Islam. In the report the ruler carries it out, and Bukhārī places it under a procedure of asking the person to repent. That is court and ruler context (rule 5, exclusion a). Its own words give no private person a licence, so it decides no label. Classical doctrine on a private person who kills an apostate (no retaliation, at most a discretionary penalty for overstepping the ruler) is given in the reconciliation. If a counted text stated that doctrine, it would bear on K1 under rules 2 and 5.

rows.reference: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 6915 (Book of Blood Money); the same saying appears in the sheet of ʿAlī at Bukhārī 111
rows.original: لاَ يُقْتَلُ مُسْلِمٌ بِكَافِرٍ
rows.translation: M. Muhsin Khan, on Sunnah.com
rows.says: A Muslim is not killed in retaliation for killing a non-Muslim (kāfir).
rows.bearing: This is graded protection, not permission (rule 2). The killer still owes blood money, and killing a protected non-Muslim is a grave sin (Bukhārī 3166). In the majority classical view no retaliation applies even for a protected non-Muslim. The Ḥanafī school does apply retaliation for a protected non-Muslim, but this is reported only through secondary scholarship. The penalty itself is court context (rule 5). The text limits equal protection under K1 but does not contradict it.

rows.says: From memory, unchecked: Moses' companion kills a boy (ghulām). Moses protests: you have killed an innocent soul who had killed no one; you have done a dreadful thing (18:74). The companion later explains that the boy's parents were believers and he feared the boy would burden them with rebellion and disbelief, so God would give them a better child (18:80 to 81). He says he did not act on his own command (18:82).
rows.bearing: This Tier 1 text, accepted by all branches, approves within the story the killing of a child who was attacking no one; the teacher in the text says the act was right (the exception in rule 4). But the killer is presented as acting on God's command and on hidden knowledge, not on his own authority. Moses' objection states the general norm. The tradition's own counted text (Muslim 1812) and its commentators confine the act to knowledge no one else can have, so it permits nothing to anyone else. It is a hard case under rule 6. It would make K1 Unclear only if the method treats a divine command to a figure with hidden knowledge as 'own authority'; otherwise it does not bear on K1. Whether ghulām here means a child or a youth is debated (unverified). No bearing on K0 or K3. Unverified, so it decides nothing now (rule 1).

counter.reconciliation:
Islam reconciles its hard texts in layers. Each authority's standing is given below. Unless a citation is marked verified, it is unverified in this run.

(1) The Qur'an (Tier 1, all branches) is the base. No soul God has made sacred may be killed except 'by right' (6:151, 17:33). Killing one soul unjustly is like killing all humankind (5:32). The heir of a murdered person has authority but must not exceed the lawful measure (17:33). Killing children, including newborn girls, is condemned (17:31, 81:8 to 9). Justice is owed even to people one hates (5:8, verified), and fairness to non-hostile non-Muslims (60:8, verified). The one Qur'anic story that approves a killing of a boy (18:74 to 82) restates the rule through Moses' objection ('an innocent soul who had killed no one'), and the killer says he did not act on his own command (18:82).

(2) Counted Sunni hadith (Sunnah, treated as primary). Bukhārī 6878 defines 'by right' as three court penalties. Ibn ʿAbbās (Muslim 1812) forbids killing children and says no one may follow al-Khaḍir's example without his knowledge. Muslim 1498 refuses a husband any private killing without four witnesses. Bukhārī 3015 and Muslim 1731 forbid killing women and children in war. Bukhārī 4339 has the Prophet disown Khālid's killing of people trying to submit. Killing a non-Muslim under treaty is a grave sin (Bukhārī 3166, verified). Bukhārī 6915 (verified) withholds retaliation for a non-Muslim victim; the Ḥanafī school, a classical school of law, applies retaliation where the victim was a protected non-Muslim (secondary report).

(3) Classical jurists and commentators (later authorities; decision 7: they count as reconciliation but never outweigh a counted text). The Sunni schools and the Twelver jurists hold that fixed penalties, including those for apostasy and for insulting the Prophet, belong to the ruler or judge after proof. Bukhārī's chapter heading for 6922 places apostasy within a procedure of asking the person to repent (verified). But the same law commonly holds that a private person who kills someone 'whose blood is forfeit' is not killed in retaliation and is at most punished at the ruler's discretion for overstepping him. That is graded protection under rule 2, unless a counted text itself declares the killing blameless.

Abū Dāwūd 4361 to 4362 are such texts if confirmed: the Prophet declares no retaliation or blood money for a woman killed privately for insulting him. Classical commentators (al-Khaṭṭābī, Maʿālim al-Sunan; the Ḥanbalī Ibn Taymiyya, al-Ṣārim al-Maslūl) are reported to take these as proof that an insulter of the Prophet may be killed and that the killer owes nothing. The Ḥanafī school is reported to hold that a protected non-Muslim's insult does not by itself end his protection.

For Twelver Shia, al-Kāfī is reported to contain reports letting anyone who hears a born Muslim renounce Islam, or anyone who hears the Prophet insulted, kill the speaker before the matter reaches the imam. Later Shia jurists are reported to condition this on no harm to the killer or others. Twelver jurists also classically hold that offensive war requires the infallible Imam, and Nahj al-Balāgha (Letters 14 and 53; Sermon 61) restrains bloodshed, killing the fleeing and wounded, and fighting the Kharijites.

On war, al-Nawawī and Ibn Ḥajar (Sunni hadith commentators, listed in corpus.md for reconciliation) reconcile 'they are of them' (Bukhārī 3012) with the ban on killing women and children by reading it as unintended harm. On captives, commentators dispute whether 47:4 (favour or ransom, verified) limits the ruler or was abrogated. The Qurayẓa killings are explained as a judicial sentence for treason.

(4) Modern bodies (outside the corpus). The 2014 Open Letter of more than 120 scholars is reported to forbid killing the innocent and to call jihad defensive. Many modern scholars and states reserve every penalty to courts. These sources do not outweigh a counted text (decision 7).

Net: the counted texts give a strong general prohibition and forbid private honour killing, infanticide, and the killing of women and children in war. The crux for K1 is the small set of texts, Sunni (Abū Dāwūd 4361 to 4362) and apparently Shia (al-Kāfī), in which a private killing of a person who insulted the Prophet or left Islam is declared blameless or permitted. Here the tradition's main reconciliation is later doctrine reserving execution to the ruler, and that doctrine still leaves the private killer largely unpunished.

K1.reason: Rule 1: only verified counted texts decide. The verified counter-evidence is context or graded protection only. Bukhārī 6922 (apostasy) and Muslim 1844a (a rival claimant) are court or ruler context (rule 5), and Bukhārī 6915 is graded protection (rule 2), answered by Bukhārī 3166 (verified). No verified text contradicts K1. The decisive leads are unverified because no search could run. Abū Dāwūd 4361: if al-Albānī's ṣaḥīḥ grade is confirmed, it counts for Sunni Islam (decision 5). In it a master kills his slave woman on his own authority for insulting the Prophet, and the Prophet declares her blood hadar (no retaliation, no blood money). That is the case rule 2 names (wholly unpunished because of what the victim did), done privately (rule 5), so K1 would be Contradicted in one branch (Sunni; rule 3). It drops to Unclear (rule 6) if the tradition's commentators read the Prophet's ruling as judicial, or require a discretionary penalty for preempting the ruler. Twelver Shia: al-Kāfī reports, if verified and graded reliable, let whoever hears an apostate or an insulter of the Prophet kill him, which would contradict K1 for that branch too, through its own texts. Qur'an 18:74 to 82 (al-Khaḍir) is a Tier 1 hard case: the killing is presented as done at God's command, not on the killer's own authority, and Muslim 1812 confines it. It bears on K1 only if the method counts a divine command as 'own authority', and then only as Unclear. The Ibadi branch and the Qur'an-only minority were not checked; for the Qur'an-only minority, 18:74 to 82 is the only hard text found.

K0.label: Not settled on verified evidence. Provisionally Taught (pending verification of Qur'an 5:32, 6:151, 17:33 and 5:27 to 31); Unclear if Abū Dāwūd 4361 is confirmed and read as a killing out of anger or revenge.
K0.reason: Verified K0 evidence: Qur'an 4:94 condemns killing for gain ('seeking the goods of this life') at Clear teaching level, though in a war setting. Bukhārī 3166 makes killing a protected non-Muslim a grave sin. Qur'an 2:194 with 42:40 allows only proportionate requital and prefers pardon. The general prohibitions (5:32, 6:151, 17:33) and the story of Adam's sons (killing out of envy, 5:27 to 31) are likely Explicit or Clear teaching for all branches but are unverified here (rule 1). No counted text was found approving a killing for gain, anger or hatred. The hard texts (Abū Dāwūd 4361 to 4362; the al-Kāfī reports) present killings as punishing an insult or apostasy, not as personal anger or revenge. Whether K0 reaches such killings is a question of reach (rule 6), so they would make K0 Unclear rather than Contradicted. Note for the method: as worded, K0 may leave private 'religious penalty' killings outside its scope altogether. Qur'an 17:33 and 2:178 route the heir's revenge through law (court context, rule 5).

K3.label: Not settled on verified evidence. Provisionally Unclear for those who have surrendered and for captives (Qurayẓa; Qur'an 47:4 disputed); taught in part, in both branches, for women and children.
K3.reason: Verified: Qur'an 47:4 names release by favour or ransom for captives (Clear teaching on one reading; whether the ruler may also kill captives is disputed), and 4:94 forbids killing one who offers peace for booty. Unverified: Bukhārī 3015 and Muslim 1731 (no killing women or children), Abū Dāwūd 2669 (no killing women or hired labourers, 'she was not one who would fight'), Bukhārī 4339 (the Prophet disowns killing people who were submitting), Nahj al-Balāgha Letter 14 and al-Kāfī (Shia: no killing of the fleeing, the wounded, women, children or the old). Taken together these would make K3 taught in part, in both branches, for women, children and the old. Hard texts: Bukhārī 3012 ('they are of them') is reconciled as unintended harm in night raids, so it does not contradict. The Qurayẓa reports (Bukhārī 3043, Abū Dāwūd 4404) approve the killing of men who had surrendered to judgement, which the tradition reads as a judicial sentence for treason; with that dispute over war versus court, rule 6 gives Unclear. Classical law's option to execute adult male captives, and one Shāfiʿī view permitting the killing of non-fighting adult men, point the same way (unverified). Qur'an 9:5 is war context about whom to fight.

rows.says: Retaliation is prescribed for the slain: the free for the free, the slave for the slave, the female for the female; the victim's family may forgive and take compensation, a mercy; in retaliation there is life (2:178 to 179). The Torah prescribed a life for a life, and whoever forgoes it, it is an expiation for him (5:45). rows.reference: Sunan Abī Dāwūd 4361 (Book of Prescribed Punishments, chapter on one who insults the Prophet); parallel Sunan al-Nasāʾī 4070 (number reported; not confirmed)
rows.original: أَلَا اشْهَدُوا أَنَّ دَمَهَا هَدَرٌ (from memory, unchecked)
rows.translation: Ahmad Hasan, on Sunnah.com, intended; not seen in this pass
rows.says: A blind man's slave woman, the mother of his children (umm walad), kept insulting the Prophet and would not stop when told. One night he killed her with a dagger. When he confessed, the Prophet said: bear witness that her blood is hadar, meaning no retaliation and no blood money are owed.
rows.bearing: The decisive Sunni text. A private person (a master in his own household) kills on his own authority, outside any court, and the Prophet declares the killing wholly free of liability because of what the victim said. That is the case rule 2 names, done privately, so rule 5's exclusion does not cover it. If its grade and content are confirmed: K1 Contradicted in one branch (Sunni; rule 3). It would fall to Unclear only if a verified listed authority (al-Nawawī, Ibn Ḥajar, Ibn Rajab) or a counted text treats the Prophet's declaration as making the killing judicial (rule 5, last sentence) or narrows it (rule 6). The commentators reported on it (al-Khaṭṭābī, Maʿālim al-Sunan; Ibn Taymiyya, al-Ṣārim al-Maslūl; both outside the listed authorities) read it as confirming that the insulter may be killed and the killer owes nothing, which widens rather than narrows; the majority rule that a private killer of one 'whose blood is forfeit' gets a discretionary penalty for overstepping the ruler is later doctrine, which never outweighs a counted text (decision 7). K0: Unclear (rule 6), since whether a killing to punish an insult counts as 'anger' or 'revenge' is a question of K0's reach. No bearing on K3. Unverified, so it decides nothing now (rule 1).

rows.says: Moses' companion kills a boy (ghulām). Moses protests: you have killed an innocent soul who killed no one; a dreadful thing (18:74). The companion later explains that the boy's parents were believers and he feared the boy would burden them with rebellion and disbelief, so God would give them a better child (18:80 to 81), and that he did not act on his own command (18:82).
rows.bearing: A Tier 1 text accepted by all branches in which the teacher within the story says the killing of a boy who attacked no one was right (rule 4's exception). But the killer expressly disclaims his own authority and acts on God's command and hidden knowledge, so K1, which binds those acting on their own authority, does not reach it as worded; Moses' objection restates the general norm. Muslim 1812 confines the act to knowledge no one else has. A hard case: Unclear (rule 6) only if the method treats a divine command to a figure with hidden knowledge as 'own authority'. Whether ghulām means a child or a youth is debated (unverified). Decides nothing now (rule 1).

rows.original: مَنْ بَدَّلَ دِينَهُ فَاقْتُلُوهُ
rows.translation: M. Muhsin Khan, on Sunnah.com
rows.says: ʿAlī, as caliph, burned some people. Ibn ʿAbbās said he would not have burned them, because punishing with fire is forbidden, but would have killed them, because the Prophet said: whoever changes his religion, kill him.
rows.bearing: A death penalty for leaving Islam, carried out in the report by the ruler and placed by Bukhārī under a procedure of asking the person to repent: context (a), rule 5. Its own words give no private licence, so it decides no label. The classical rule that a private killer of an apostate faces at most a discretionary penalty is later doctrine; it would bear on K1 only if a counted text stated it (the al-Kāfī apostate report is such a candidate for the Shia branch).

rows.reference: Qur'an 9:5, read with 9:4 and 9:6 (Sūrat al-Tawba); 8:61 (Sūrat al-Anfāl)
rows.original: فَاقْتُلُوا الْمُشْرِكِينَ حَيْثُ وَجَدتُّمُوهُمْ ... وَإِنْ أَحَدٌ مِّنَ الْمُشْرِكِينَ اسْتَجَارَكَ فَأَجِرْهُ (from memory, unchecked)
rows.translation: Pickthall intended; not seen in this pass
rows.says: When the sacred months have passed, slay the idolaters wherever you find them, take and besiege them; if they repent, pray and give alms, let them go (9:5). Treaty partners who kept faith are excepted (9:4). If an idolater asks for protection, grant it so he may hear God's word, then take him to safety (9:6). If they incline to peace, incline to it too (8:61).
rows.bearing: War context (b), rule 5; does not decide K1. For K3, 9:5 concerns whom to fight; commentators are reported to tie it to treaty-breaking Arab polytheists of that time, limited by 9:4 and 9:6, and to dispute whether it abrogated gentler verses (47:4, 60:8) (unverified). 9:6 is Clear teaching to protect a non-fighter who asks for safety, if verified. The classical schools are reported to differ on killing non-fighting adult men (most protect them; one Shāfiʿī view allows it), and Twelver jurists to hold that offensive war needs the presence of the infallible Imam (all unverified).
rows.strength: n/a (K1); Clear teaching for 9:6 (K3, if verified)

rows.reference: Qur'an 8:67 to 69 (Sūrat al-Anfāl), with Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 1763 (Book of Jihad and Expeditions; the captives of Badr)
rows.original: مَا كَانَ لِنَبِيٍّ أَن يَكُونَ لَهُ أَسْرَىٰ حَتَّىٰ يُثْخِنَ فِي الْأَرْضِ (8:67, from memory, unchecked)
rows.translation: Pickthall and A. H. Siddiqui intended; not seen in this pass
rows.says: It is not for a prophet to hold captives until he has made a great slaughter in the land; you desire the goods of this world (8:67). After Badr the Prophet took Abū Bakr's advice to accept ransom for the captives rather than ʿUmar's advice to kill them, and the verse came down agreeing with ʿUmar; 8:69 then lets the Muslims enjoy what they took (Muslim 1763).
rows.bearing: A hard text for K3 on captives: within the account, God's word reproves sparing captives for ransom in that battle. Commentators are reported to dispute whether 47:4 (favour or ransom) abrogated 8:67 or the reverse, and classical law let the ruler choose among killing, enslaving, ransom or release (unverified). With 47:4 and the Qurayẓa reports, the treatment of captives is disputed: Unclear for K3 (rule 6). War context only for K1. Neither researcher analysed it (the counter researcher listed 8:67 without comment).

rows.says: After a siege, Banū Qurayẓa surrendered to the judgement of Saʿd ibn Muʿādh, who ruled that their fighting men be killed and their women and children taken captive; the Prophet said he had judged with God's judgement. rows.translation: Sahih International (legacy.quran.com, 5:8); Quran.com English (60:8)

verified.reconciliation:
How Islam reconciles its texts on killing, with each authority's standing. Unless marked verified, every citation here is unverified in this pass.

1. The Qur'an (Tier 1, all branches) is the base. It forbids killing 'a soul' (5:32), 'the soul God has made sacred, except by right' (6:151; 17:33; 25:68), and one's own children, newborn girls included (6:140; 6:151; 17:31; 60:12; 81:8 to 9). The heir of one wrongly killed has authority but must not exceed the limit (17:33), and retaliation is prescribed to the community with pardon preferred (2:178 to 179; 5:45; 42:40, verified). Justice is owed even to hated people (5:8, verified) and fairness to non-hostile non-Muslims (60:8, verified). The one Qur'anic story that approves the killing of a boy (18:74 to 82) restates the rule through Moses' objection, and the killer says he did not act on his own command (18:82).

2. The Sunnah (counted for Sunni Islam). Bukhārī 6878 = Muslim 1676 = Forty no. 14 defines 'by right' as three penalties that classical law gives to a court. Bukhārī 3166 (verified) makes killing a covenanted non-Muslim a grave sin, which is the tradition's own answer to Bukhārī 6915 (verified): no retaliation for a non-Muslim victim, in the majority view, is graded protection, not permission (rule 2); the Ḥanafī school applies retaliation for a protected non-Muslim (secondary report). The same pattern, graded protection, covers a father who kills his child (Tirmidhī 1400, grade to confirm) and a master who kills his slave (2:178 as classically read; Abū Dāwūd 4515 = Tirmidhī 1414, with disputed grades, would forbid it outright). Muslim 1498 denies a husband any private killing without four witnesses, and the oath procedure of 24:6 to 9 replaces killing (Bukhārī 5259); the praise of Saʿd's jealousy (Muslim 1498c; Bukhārī 6846) is reported to be read by al-Nawawī and Ibn Ḥajar (listed commentators) as praise of jealousy, not permission. Ibn ʿAbbās (Muslim 1812) forbids killing children and says no one may follow al-Khaḍir's example. Abū Bakr's saying that killing for an insult 'was not for anyone after Muḥammad' (Abū Dāwūd 4363, grade to confirm) confines any such killing to insults against the Prophet himself.

3. The hard texts. Abū Dāwūd 4361 (and 4362) has the Prophet declaring 'not to be avenged' a private killing of a woman who insulted him. The commentators reported on it, al-Khaṭṭābī and Ibn Taymiyya (both outside the listed authorities), read it as confirming that such a person may be killed and the killer owes nothing. The majority classical doctrine reserves the penalty to the ruler and gives a private killer of one 'whose blood is forfeit' a discretionary penalty for overstepping him (iftiyāt ʿalā al-imām), but that is later doctrine and never outweighs a counted text (decision 7). No reconciliation by a listed authority (al-Nawawī, Ibn Ḥajar, Ibn Rajab) was found or verified. For Twelver Shia, al-Kāfī is reported to contain reports letting whoever hears a born Muslim renounce Islam, or hears the Prophet insulted, kill the speaker before the matter reaches the imam; Twelver jurists are reported to keep this with a condition of safety, which narrows but does not remove it. Nahj al-Balāgha (Letters 14 and 53; Sermon 61; Shia) restrains bloodshed, the killing of the fleeing and wounded, and fighting the Kharijites, but does not address these reports.

4. War. Bukhārī 3015, Muslim 1731 and Abū Dāwūd 2669 forbid killing women, children and hired workers ('she was not one who would fight'); Bukhārī 4339 has the Prophet disown Khālid's killing of people who were submitting; 4:90 and 4:94 (verified) protect those who offer peace. Bukhārī 3012 ('they are of them') is reported to be read by al-Nawawī and Ibn Ḥajar as unintended harm in night raids. Captives are the unresolved point: 47:4 (verified) names only release by favour or ransom, but 8:67 with Muslim 1763, the Qurayẓa judgement (Bukhārī 3043; Muslim 1768; Abū Dāwūd 4404) and classical law's option to execute male captives point the other way; commentators dispute which verse abrogated which.

5. Modern bodies (outside the corpus). The 2014 Open Letter of more than 120 scholars is reported to forbid killing the innocent and vigilante punishment; modern states and many fatwa bodies reserve every penalty to courts. These do not count and do not outweigh a counted text.

Net: the counted texts give a strong general ban, forbid infanticide, private honour killing and the killing of women and children in war, and grade rather than lift protection for non-Muslims, slaves and children killed by parents. The crux for K1 is a small set of texts, Sunni (Abū Dāwūd 4361 to 4362) and reportedly Twelver Shia (al-Kāfī), in which a private killing of a person who insulted the Prophet or left Islam is declared unpunished or permitted. The tradition's main answer, that such penalties belong to the ruler, is later doctrine, not a counted text, and it still leaves the private killer without retaliation.

Abū Dāwūd 4363 bears on that question without settling it, and the commentators reported on 4361 widen rather than narrow it. (b) Twelver Shia: the al-Kāfī reports on the apostate and on one who insults the Prophet, if confirmed and graded reliable, let a private hearer kill before the matter reaches the imam: Contradicted in one branch (Twelver Shia; rule 3). Other hard cases do not change this: Qur'an 17:33 (heir's authority) is court context if classical law's requirement of a judge holds, otherwise Unclear; Qur'an 18:74 to 82 bears on K1 only if a divine command to a figure with hidden knowledge counts as 'own authority'; Muslim 140 and Bukhārī 6902 limit the defence exception without contradicting it. Qur'an 4:94 (verified) condemns killing for gain ('seeking the goods of this life') at Clear teaching level, but it is a war text (rule 5), so it supports without deciding. If verified, the Qur'an teaches K0 Explicitly or by Clear teaching for all branches: the general bans (5:32; 6:151; 17:33; 25:68), killing children because of poverty or fear of it (6:151; 17:31; Bukhārī 4477), killing a brother out of rivalry (5:27 to 31), killing joined to aggression and unjust gain (4:29 to 30), and excess in revenge (17:33); the Farewell Sermon (Muslim 1218a, these passages unverified) cancels blood feud. No counted text was found approving a killing for gain, anger, hatred or private revenge. The hard texts (Abū Dāwūd 4361 to 4362; the al-Kāfī reports) present killings as punishing an insult or apostasy. Whether K0's 'anger, hatred or revenge' reaches such killings is a question of reach, so if they are confirmed K0 becomes Unclear in the branch concerned (rule 6), not Contradicted. Method note: as worded, K0 may leave private 'religious penalty' killings outside its scope altogether, which weakens it as a floor.

K3 names children, the old, civilians and those who have surrendered, so this is taught in part (rule 7). If confirmed, women and children are covered in the Sunni branch, and in the Shia branch children and the old rest only on the al-Kāfī report; the old are not covered in counted Sunni texts (Abū Dāwūd 2614 is reported weak). Unverified hard texts: the Qurayẓa judgement (Bukhārī 3043; Muslim 1768; Abū Dāwūd 4404) approves killing men who had surrendered to judgement, and the tradition reads it as a judicial sentence for breaking a treaty; Qur'an 8:67 with Muslim 1763 reproves sparing the Badr captives for ransom; classical law let the ruler execute male captives. With the war-or-court character disputed and 47:4 and 8:67 in tension, rule 6 gives Unclear for surrendered fighters and captives once these are verified. Bukhārī 3012 is read as unintended harm (night raids), so it does not contradict. K3 is a record wording, so no floor depends on it.

verified.fairness_notes:
1. The result on verified evidence ('taught in part') comes from a verification outage, not from the texts. The Qur'an's bans on killing (5:32; 6:151; 17:31; 17:33; 25:68; 81:8 to 9) are among the most explicit Tier 1 bans in any of the thirteen traditions. If other traditions are labelled from verified Tier 1 bans while Islam's stay unverified, an adherent would rightly see a different outcome caused by process. Islam's Qur'anic rows should be verified before any comparison is published.
2. Islam is tested on a larger counted corpus than most traditions: every Sunni hadith graded sound or good by any recognised scholar (decision 5), plus al-Kāfī for the Shia branch. That raises the chance of finding one contradicting report, compared with traditions whose counted corpus is a single short book. This follows the corpus decisions, but it should be stated beside the result.
3. Conflicting hadith grades must be handled by one rule. If al-Albānī's ṣaḥīḥ grade makes Abū Dāwūd 4361 count against K1, al-Tirmidhī's own reported ḥasan grade should make Tirmidhī 1414 (forbidding a master to kill his slave) count for it, and vice versa. Neither researcher did this.
4. Parallel texts in other traditions must get the same treatment: Phinehas' zealot killing approved by God (Numbers 25:7 to 13; Tier 1 for Judaism and Christianity) and its rabbinic narrowing (Sanhedrin 81b to 82a), the blood avenger who kills the murderer on meeting him (Numbers 35:19 to 21) against the Qur'an's heir (17:33), the kinsman's hand 'first upon' the one who entices to other gods (Deuteronomy 13), and the blameless killing of a night thief (Exodus 22:1 in English numbering) against Muslim 140. If those are labelled Unclear because later authorities narrow them, the same must be asked of Abū Dāwūd 4361; if Abū Dāwūd 4361 is labelled Contradicted despite the classical doctrine reserving penalties to the ruler, the same standard applies to them. The Stoicism verifier applied rule 2 directly to Seneca, De Ira 1.15.2; the same reading of rule 2 is used here.
5. War texts (9:5; 47:4; 4:89; Qurayẓa) are context for K1, exactly as Deuteronomy 20, Joshua and the Bhagavad Gita are. They bear only on K3, which is a record wording.
6. Texts worded for believers (4:92 to 93; Bukhārī 6878; Bukhārī 25) should not be read as limiting protection by faith when the same corpus has general 'soul' texts and Bukhārī 3166, just as 'your neighbour' texts in other traditions are read beside their general texts.
7. Modern repudiations (the 2014 Open Letter, state law reserving penalties to courts, many fatwa bodies) do not count, as other traditions' modern bodies do not count. Saying so plainly avoids implying that Muslims today generally accept private killing for insult or apostasy: the hard texts are reported, and their status is exactly what the verification must settle.
8. K0 as worded may not reach killings presented as religious penalties, in any tradition. If that weakens K0 for Islam, it weakens it equally for Judaism, Christianity and others with similar texts.
